en: The Supplementary Ritual for the Golden Light Repentance, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zunshe of Mount Taiye in Tiantai, Song Dynasty. 1. The Origin of the Ritual.
First, regarding the origin: if one observes that prior to the actual practice there are no [sections on] the five intentions beginning with the origin, it is not the authentic version.
Question: The ritual procedures have already been recorded in the *Bai lu* (One Hundred Records),
and the contemplative wisdom is further indicated in other texts.
Regarding these two paths, what further benefit could there be? Answer:
Now, observing that the ritual procedures have already been established based on the old scriptures.
The prophetic master’s words amount to approximately one hundred records, all of which follow a single standard without any separate establishment.
At the time of practical application, matters requiring deliberation cannot be avoided more than three or four times.
Furthermore, there is the method of the "scattered sprinkling" (san-sai).
The Sūtra says:
"Specifically, with various kinds of delicious flavors,
offer them as alms to me and sprinkle them in all directions."
At that time, one should recite these passages.
Among them, four phrases are difficult to understand:
first, there is an omission of a specific explanation regarding the offering of food and drink as a gift to the celestial maidens.
Second, there is an omission regarding the distribution and scattering of portions for the various deities;
third, there is an omission concerning the clarification of the locations where the food is scattered;
fourth, the timing of the recitation of mantras appears to be out of sequence.
This is a new translation by Master Zhun Jing;
it lacks only the third section concerning the place for scattering food,
while the rest is very clear.
The new commentary states:
"One should likewise make offerings of incense, flowers, and various foods to my image;
furthermore, one should take food and drink and scatter them toward other directions as alms for the various spirits."
The words for reciting the mantra are also set forth separately.
First, one is instructed to prostrate to the Buddha and then immediately recite the mantra;
it says "summoning and inviting," but does not say that the mantra is to be recited at the time of the *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) ritual.
Observing this new text, it supplements the old ritual format.
If that is so, the *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred Matters) instructs that one should separately arrange a single platter to be distributed to the various directions;
this accords with the new scripture as perfectly as a tally.
What is meant by "nor being established separately"?
The answer is: although it initially appears to be divided, later it reaches the state of being dispersed.
Furthermore, following the scriptural text and having them recite the mantra immediately would also result in difficulty of comprehension. Why?
Because the original purpose of the mantra was to summon celestial maidens.
It may only be done together with one's own disciples;
if it were performed by reciting at a place where people are eating separately,
it would amount to merely summoning one's own followers.
Even granting that they recite simultaneously, there is still no clear place for it;
furthermore, it would be highly inconvenient to distribute food and drink within the ritual arena (maṇḍala).
If one were to distribute them in a different location while reciting the mantra simultaneously, that too would be untenable.
Moreover, the timing for reciting mantras should likewise not be so;
one must first hold the mantra to summon the principal deity and their retinue to the ritual site.
Furthermore, when subsequently offering food and drink, it must necessarily be done in a separate location.
Moreover, in current practice, this rite is often modeled after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other Vaipulya sutras;
from the first day onward, the invitation of the Triple Gem is discontinued.
To simply recite the mantra in this manner is highly deficient in its proper sequence;
furthermore, the *Bai lu* does not include the five repentances.
Later generations have used these [texts] indiscriminately;
that they are now all supplemented is not for nothing.

Second, regarding the analysis of the text and the opening of chapters to determine the sequence: although the ritual texts of the Director of Records (Lùshì Yíwén) are extremely concise, [the following analysis is provided].
Examining its intent in detail, it is expanded into ten sections;
however, it lacks only the single section on the Five Repentances. What are these ten?
First, one should adorn and purify the chamber;
second, one should purify the three karmas;
third, one should make offerings of incense and flowers.
Fourth, the invocation of the mantra-holders;
fifth, the praise and declaration of intent;
sixth, the recitation of names and the offering of gifts.
Seventh, pay reverent homage to the Triple Gem.
Eighth, practice the fivefold repentance.
Ninth, circumambulate while taking refuge.
Tenth is the chanting and recitation of the scriptures.
This differs slightly from the sequence and arrangement in the *Bailu* (Record of a Hundred Items); by comparing them, it can be understood.
However, as for the five repentances (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*), they are now placed here according to the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions" (*Karmāvaraṇaviśuddhi-parivarta*).
However, the account of the origins of the *Jianchan* (Repentance Ritual) lacks any verses of praise.
Now, following other ritual procedures,
I have employed the "Praise of the Four Heavenly Kings" from the new translation of the sutra for this purpose.
In the Vaipulya and Lotus Sutras, there are both seated meditation and vocal recitation;
this text, however, prescribes only the latter.
I believe there is a profound intention behind this and do not dare to alter it.
If that is so, does the non-inclusion of the five types of repentance (pañca-deśanā) also have a specific intention?
The answer is: this should not be treated as an analogy; it is merely an abbreviation in the text.
Or it is said:
To claim that one should stop reciting at the "Chapter on Repentance" (Sāṃghāṭī-prakaraṇa) and simply perform repentance is also incorrect;
it should rather be combined with the "Chapter on the Extinction of Obstacles" (Āvaraṇa-vināśana-prakaraṇa).
For each individual confession, one must first perform the full ritual of reverence before making the disclosure;
it should be understood that these must be performed separately.

3. A Separate Explanation of the Two Methods of Prostration-Invitation and Sprinkling-Dispersion. Third: It should be understood that this method is identical to the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara, taking invocation as its practice.
For seven days and six periods, one must perform the ritual invitations one after another,
according to the *Bai lu fang deng yi* (The Ritual Manual for the Vaipulya Scriptures) and the *Lotus Samādhi*.
All [the texts] conclude by stating that for the latter six periods, the invocation of the Buddha is omitted;
otherwise, the remaining nine rites are performed without difference.

Only in the invocations of Avalokiteśvara and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is there no such concluding statement, which can be understood as a point of reference. Furthermore, upon examining the ritual procedures for the spells of Mahāprajñā, Dṛḍhanārāyaṇa, Samantabhadra, Vaiśravaṇa, and others in the new translations [of the scriptures], [one finds the same].
They all exclusively take invocation as their primary practice.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Heavenly Maidens" states:
"For my sake, recite the names of the Triple Gem three times every day."
I truly invite the Great Auspicious Goddess.
When you recite the divine mantra and summon me, having heard the invocation of the divine mantra, I shall come.
"I have already arrived at that place.
Since it is thus for the three times of day, one should know by analogy that it is the same for the three times of night.
Moreover, the subsequent text says:
Furthermore, if you recite and maintain the aforementioned mantra during the late afternoon,
my arrival will surely be as you hope; yet,
there are often those who do not understand the ritual procedures for practicing Avalokiteśvara.
I also wish to cancel the request;
this is a great matter of which I am ignorant.
For now, I shall merely compile a brief summary of the petitions from the *Baolu* (Records of the Hundred).
All constitute five stages; they are merely different ways of opening and closing [the categories].
Therefore, it is not a matter of deletion or reduction, which is why they are combined.
It is easy to prepare food and drink for a morning meal;
as for extensive invitations at other times beyond midday,
there should likewise be no such thing.
Please observe that in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, there is no such instruction; one must not arbitrarily omit it.
Second, regarding the sprinkling and scattering [of water]:
in principle, one must separately designate a pure area outside the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).
Alternatively, one may construct a small altar and sprinkle it everywhere with fragrant liquid,
ensuring it is strictly pure and clean; then, placing an object beneath the feet,
one stands in its center and performs circumambulation.
The fourth [method] is to pass through by eating until one is completely exhausted.
Question: From what text does this derive?
Answer: It is simply not mentioned in either of the two sutras in the *Baolu* (Records of the Hundred).
This was edited by my own judgment with the sole aim of generating wholesome merit;
truly, there is no fault in this.
I await seeing other texts so that I may revise it according to the established tradition; it will not be too late.
4. A Brief Clarification of the Petitioner and the Sought Free from Faults. Fourth, based on the three meanings of the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*:
first, requesting for one's own sake.
The second is requesting for the sake of others;
the third is requesting for the sake of protecting the True Dharma.
Now, according to the intent of this chapter, the primary focus lies in protecting the Dharma.
This is the *Devatāparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
Thirdly, one should dedicate merit for the sake of requesting the teaching and for those who listen to it.
In general, one should also possess all three.
As the Sūtra says:
"One should act for the sake of oneself and for the sake of all sentient beings."
This is precisely both for oneself and for others.
To cause this sublime sutra to circulate widely is itself the protection of the Dharma.
These are all merely the text of this very chapter.
Furthermore, the new edition states:
"If you can circulate this sutra, it will benefit both yourself and others."
This is the explicit text.
He himself requested its restoration three times.
First, he extended the invitation.
Second is the prayer of invocation; third is the prayer of aspiration.
These correspond to the three karmas to constitute the capacity for awakening.
The chapter states:
"To bathe one's body, prostrate, and make offerings constitutes the physical act of invitation."
To recite mantras to summon me is the oral action of supplication;
it is to make a vow with utmost sincerity.
This refers to the invitation through the mental action (*manas-karman*).
For the sake of protecting the Dharma for others, the three actions are likewise so.
The invitation is further threefold.
This section sets forth the request for realization through the application of the mind;
"setting forth the mind" means that when one focuses the will with sincere devotion and makes a petition, a response is evoked.
The new edition states:
One should make an invitation with truthful words and give rise to the aspiration for what is sought.
Regarding the practitioner, even if they do not explicitly direct their mind toward it, the Great Sage will naturally respond to them, provided that their three karmas are pure.
The chapter states:
"I shall, for the rest of my life, never distance myself from such a person.
Regarding the requester, the *Ghosts and Spirits* chapter states:
If one enters this sutra, one enters the dharma-nature;
within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni.
Since the invitation is thus, the aspiration is likewise so.

For these sentient beings of the ten realms, who possess such karmic conditions of the three modes of action and whose two types of perfection remain unfulfilled, [the Buddha’s response is accordingly].
To protect the Dharma for the sake of others, one must certainly extend an invitation.
Second, regarding the clarification of the faults to be abandoned from what is sought, it is asked:
The *Bai lu* states:
"Regarding the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual,
one should simply subdue the mind and repent for transgressions."
If there should suddenly arise a request,
the answer is that the principle is indeed so;
it is simply because the practice of the Dharma-activity emerges from this chapter.
With auspiciousness as its primary focus,
the intent of this chapter is further to explain the merit of both the teaching and the listening.
This is the textual content within the chapter.
Most [versions] clarify the wealth and treasures while speaking little of repentance;
only the new edition states:
"Making offerings to all Buddhas, one personally confesses one's own transgressions."
Regarding the dedication of merit, the making of vows, and so forth,
this chapter further clarifies the increase of wealth and possessions;
for this reason, one often incurs the flattery and attachment of others.
To avoid this fault, he demonstrates what is sought.
Now, two interpretations are presented.
First, if one simply repents with a pure mind and seeks nothing else;
Relying exclusively on the principles of fact and reason with single-minded diligence—
whether grasping at signs or contemplating emptiness—
if one intends to extinguish transgressions through such means, this is not what is being discussed here.
Second, if one seeks to protect the Dharma or requests its exposition, one must first set the mind upon the goal of what is sought.
The practitioner must clearly recognize its faults;
furthermore, there are two further intentions.
First, regarding the three requests, the point of origin for faults is shown:
namely, that in both practice and realization, the two types of request must be free from deceit.
If there is deceit, practice itself is not established, and thus it cannot produce its result.
Regarding those who merely perform the ritual by designating their intention (*citta*),
faults arise because there may be both authenticity and falsehood in the matter.
This second point specifically concerns designating the intention to examine for such faults.
Furthermore, there are two parts:
first, a brief presentation of the correct [view] by means of three meanings;
second, the refutation of errors by contrasting them with this [correct view].
Third, regarding the capacity of those who request [the teaching]:
this refers to those who truly desire to penetrate the sutra—
whether they be the requester, the speaker, or the listener.
Whenever there is a deficiency, the flow of the Dharma becomes obstructed.
Setting one's mind upon this and designating a specific object of focus, one should pray with devotion for seven days.
Since one wishes to rely on celestial power, it is appropriate that the results far exceed expectations.
Please speak with sincerity;
speak until you have reached full understanding;
listen with diligence.
The others are not capable of producing [the result].
Second, regarding the Sage who is able to respond,
this is the Auspicious Mahādeva.
The mind of Heaven does not deceive; its words are indeed true.
Though it responds without prior consultation, there is not even a hair’s breadth of error.
Once the true pivot is struck, the wondrous response is immediately attained. Thus it is.
Third, regarding the intention of bestowing wealth:
the intention lies in moistening that place and making a request;
by fulfilling their lack, one increases their joy.
Providing them with the necessary provisions and allowing them to teach for a long time.
As the Sūtra says:
"This Dharma-preacher..."
I shall provide for them so that their minds may abide in peace;
day and night they shall rejoice, maintaining right mindfulness and contemplating the profound meaning.
This same principle applies to those who invite [the teacher] and those who listen.
Therefore, it is not for those who are mediocre or dull-witted,
who eat their fill all day long without applying their minds to anything;
that Heaven bestows wealth upon them.
Next, regarding those who have transcended [the world],
it may be understood by reversing the preceding account;
furthermore, it shall be explained briefly once more.
Furthermore, a son of the renunciant life should not even seek the precepts, worldly dhyāna,
or the wisdom of the two vehicles.
How could it be permissible to make no use of the Way at all,
but instead devote oneself solely to nourishing the physical body,
sycophantically following outward rituals while secretly scheming for wealth and profit?
If one continues to amass many possessions, one violates strict precepts;
the eight impure riches invite suffering in the three evil realms.
Regarding offerings, there is no merit, as stated in the *Five Hundred Questions*: [text omitted].
One cannot even avoid the hells;
how much less can one hope for the attainment of blessings? Once these are established, they are ultimately empty.
If you intend to seek rebirth in the heavens, I fear that such a day will never come.
Second, Heaven assists those with virtue and does not bless those who lack the Way.
One who hoards wealth while violating the precepts is abandoned by Heaven and censured by men.
If one merely desires to offer earnest prayers, the more one draws near, the further one becomes;
even now that the great demons have cleared their tracks,
how could one hope for the Honored Heaven to protect the person?
"O Heaven! It shows no partiality; it assists only those who possess virtue.
How could I, in my pursuit of the common and base, speak of never again distancing myself from this man for the rest of my life?"
Thirdly, since they have already opposed the will of Heaven,
what is the use of wealth?
My intention is to propagate the Classics, not merely to sustain my life.
If one even causes accumulated wealth to be dispersed, how could one allow it to increase greed?
Furthermore, since the Dharma of the śramaṇas already censures defilement,
who would praise the hoarding of property?
In this world, there are those who lack understanding and merely seek to demand [results].
Yet the heavenly net is vast; though its mesh is wide, nothing escapes it.
It is asked:
Reflecting on what has been stated above, I fear it may not be entirely so. Why?
Because human sentiment naturally obstructs the Way of Heaven, whereas the principle of Heaven is fundamentally pervasive.
The compassion of a Bodhisattva is called "unconditioned" (anālambana).
A Great Being bestows universal salvation;
even a bandit who recites the Buddha’s name obtains a golden head—
how much more so a monk who serves the celestial spirit, yet begrudges offerings of jade and silk?
I answer you: your question shows a profound lack of understanding.
It is like the law of a state:
if a minister commits an illegal act, he incurs punishment.
Having been dismissed from office and deprived of his stipend, he instead rebuked the ruler, saying:
"The Son of Heaven is benevolent and compassionate; he should not show partiality.
His grace should extend even to grasses and trees, and his bounty reach the orphaned and the poor."
Why are you stingy with rank and emolument toward your ministers?
Consider this reprimand: is he not a wise minister?
The Sūtra states that one who can uphold even a single phrase or a chapter title [is a true upholder].
"By means of wealth and by means of protection" refers to the inclusion of lay followers and the manifestation of the merit of upholding [the teachings].
Artisans, merchants, officials, and farmers each seek their respective forms of wealth.
Even kings, ministers, and elders who provide for their nations and enrich their families must be made to listen to this sutra and be required to practice it together.
As stated in the "Earth Deity" Chapter:
He delighted in practicing generosity with a mind always firm;
he had deep faith in the Triple Gem and could accumulate wealth only to disperse it in charity.
From youth, he had heard of the reputation of the incorruptible scholar.
Content with little and moderate in measure,
he has long admired the model of the practitioner;
yet, though his reputation was known, he had not yet seen him in person.
One whose will is defiled and mixed with that of ordinary people is one whom humans seek and the heavens protect. 5.

A General Demonstration of the Basis for Contemplative Wisdom Regarding Phenomena and Principle. Fifth. This present text is based primarily on the *Baolu* (Record of the Hundred Matters) as well as the two new and old sutras.
I have collated passages from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* to establish ten sections of ritual procedures; however,
there is a lack of preparatory expedients prior to the actual cultivation.
This is explained extensively in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* and various repentance rituals (*pūjā-vidhi*).
Those who wish to practice this should seek out the commentary on the "Chapter on Repentance."
One should first clearly understand the locus of repentance and the methods of repentance; one must know precisely each of the primary and auxiliary dharmas.
If one encounters the images of the Honored Ones or ritual implements, one should practice contemplative wisdom through these successive activities.
One should seek out the texts for the Fangdeng Repentance (Vaipulya Repentance) concerning Samatha and Vipasyanā.
If one intends to perform the meditative visualizations following each of the ten sections of the ritual procedures from beginning to end,
one should consult the *Fahua Zuboyi* (Supplementary Ritual for the Lotus Sutra).
Furthermore, one must recite them thoroughly so that the mental application proceeds without obstruction.
This applies to the texts concerning the sutras, dharanis, Buddha names, the five repentances, and so forth.
One must also pre-recite [the texts] until they are thoroughly mastered;
one should not continue to read from the written text while inside the ritual arena (maṇḍala).
Furthermore, one must consult the commentaries.
One clearly understands the three types of repentance methods— taking signs (*nimitta*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and the ritual procedure (*vidhi*)—
along with their general and specific aspects, the stages of phenomena and principle, their respective obstacles,
and the characteristics of their sequential depth and shallowness.
One must not fail to understand this;
be careful not to treat it lightly.
Furthermore, I exhort future students.
Whenever one intends to copy [a text],
it must be transcribed in its entirety from beginning to end;
one should collate it clearly so as not to allow omissions or errors.
I have frequently observed that in the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara* repentance liturgies,
much of the introductory and concluding sections, as well as the passages concerning insight and wisdom, have been excised.
I have merely excerpted the section on the Buddha’s rank and the text for repentance;
the fact that the title of the ritual for worship alone is so deeply lamentable—
if one is unable [to fulfill this], it would be better not to transcribe it at all.
Lest the full text of the practice be destroyed or scattered;
if even a single matter is incomplete, the characteristics of the practice will be deficient.
Deeply cautioned! Deeply cautioned!

6. Supplementary Ritual for the Ten Categories of Practice to Assist Right Cultivation Supplementary Ritual for the Ten Categories of Practice to Assist Right Cultivation, Part Six Section One: Methods for Adorning and Purifying the Site of Practice (*Mandala*) Regarding the methods for adorning and purifying the site of practice: if one is practicing in one's own dwelling place...
If one is in an araṇya (wilderness retreat),
one should carefully prepare a single room to serve as a bodhimaṇḍa,
and separately install a seat for chanting the sūtras.
This would cause the site of practice (dojang) to appear deficient.
Within the site of practice, one must install an image of Śākyamuni,
and before that image, one must install the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
To the left of the Buddha, place the seat of Śrīdevī;
according to the new sūtra,
one should paint an image of Śrīdevī.
If the site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) is spacious,
further install the seat of the Great Eloquence Four Heavenly Kings on the right side.
According to the *Vaiśravaṇa-dhāraṇī-vidhi*,
one should paint Śrī-devī to the left of the Buddha,
and depict myself, the god Vaiśravaṇa, to the right of the Buddha.
Now the site of the *bodhimaṇḍa* is even more narrow;
it would likewise be beneficial to install a seat for the deity Mahāmati (the God of Great Learning),
for the goddesses dwell in that excellent garden.
To manifest the provisional and the ultimate and for the sake of convenience, they suspended silk streamers, banners,
and canopies; they arranged offerings and adorned the various seats,
and thoroughly swept the ground.
Sprinkle fragrant liquids and smear the ground with fragrant mud.
Light various lamps filled with fragrant oils and scatter diverse, exquisite flowers upon the seats.
They offered powdered incense and various renowned types of burning incense to the Triple Gem,
providing whatever they were capable of preparing with their own strength;
they devoted their hearts and exhausted their intentions to ensure the utmost purity and solemnity.
Why is this so? Because the practitioner’s inner mind reveres the Triple Gem and transcends the three realms.
Now, as I wish to respectfully invite and make offerings,
how could I possibly act with a light-hearted mind?
If one cannot extract from one's own resources to make offerings to the Mahāyāna, [one fails in this duty].
Ultimately, they will never attract the worthy or move the sages;
their grave offenses will not be extinguished,
so by what means could roots of goodness possibly arise?

2. The Second Method for Purifying the Three Karmas: Regarding the method for purifying the three karmas, from the first day until the conclusion of the entire period, the practitioner shall bathe daily with fragrant water.
If one reaches a defiled place and has finished one's business there, one must bathe immediately.
Even if one does not encounter anything defiling for an entire day,
one must still bathe once.
One should wear clean garments, such as the outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) or newly dyed robes;
if there are no new ones, one should take the best of one's own clothes.
He should wash and dye them thoroughly to serve as robes for entering the *maṇḍala*.
Whether entering or leaving, removing or putting them on, this may be known by one's own mind.
The practitioner shall continue this for a full seven days.
One must be single-minded and avoid miscellaneous speech or all manner of social greetings and inquiries.
If one seeks what is required, one should speak directly to the matter at hand;
one must not, on account of that matter, trigger further discourse.
The practitioner shall complete the seven days,
maintaining single-minded concentration on the dharma being cultivated,
without allowing a single moment’s thought of worldly affairs.
One should maintain strict vigilance so that [unwholesome thoughts] do not arise.
Regarding the three types of action mentioned above—
whether in eating or in attending to the calls of nature— one should act with mindfulness.
Guard against loss with a single mind.
Do not make excuses or delay; you must act directly and in accordance with the matter.
3. The Third Method for Offering Incense and Flowers: When the practitioner first enters the maṇḍala, they proceed before the Dharma seat and spreads out their sitting mat (niṣīdana).
Standing upright with palms joined,
one should first cultivate thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings,
vowing to rescue and deliver them.
Next, give rise to a heart of profound reverence;
with shame and remorse, feel deep sincerity,
and maintain mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Filling the void of space,
they manifest at the site of enlightenment.
Having formed such a visualization:
Prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground,
they pay homage to all Three Jewels,
causing their reflections to appear before all Buddhas.
Having performed this prostration, the one who leads the chant says:
"With all reverence, with single-minded devotion, we pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions; our minds follow our bodies and speech."
With single-minded devotion, pay homage without distraction,
realizing that this body is as insubstantial as a shadow;
let there be no attainment of either the one who prostrates or the object of prostration within the mind.
All sentient beings likewise enter together into the ocean of prostrations to the Triple Gem;
having collectively paid homage to the Triple Gem,
they kneel with their right knees on the ground after one prostration.
Holding an incense burner in his hand,
he further chanted:
"All you members of the assembly, each kneel in the *hu* position."
Solemnly holding incense and flowers, perform offerings according to the Dharma until the chanting ceases.
Holding the flowers in your hands, silently recite the words of visualization for the offering as found in the *Fahua Zuboyi* (Supplementary Ritual for the Lotus Sutra).
One should examine that text, recite it thoroughly, and apply it.
Having directed the mind, chant:
"May these clouds of incense and flowers..."
Pervading the realms of the ten directions,
they make offerings to all Buddhas,
the Honored Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas.
The assemblies of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as all the celestial seers,
having performed the service of making offerings for the Buddha’s work, paid all their respects.

4. The Fourth Method for Invoking and Reciting Mantras: Regarding the method for invoking and reciting mantras, one should next kneel on the right knee, hold an incense burner in hand, and burn various kinds of fragrant incense.
With single-minded devotion, one should invoke the Triple Gem, as well as Śrīdevī and the others.
One should give rise to a heart of profound reverence, weeping with tears and lamenting;
one should contemplate each visualization as being present at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
These words are from the *Buzhuyi* (Supplementary Ritual).
One should inspect [the image] and speak these words with single-minded devotion:
"Homage to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha."

Having made three requests before all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time as found throughout the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, including the four World-Honored Buddhas of the East— such as Akṣobhya, Ratnakusuma, Vaidūrya-ratna-vijaya, and so forth— one should perform one prostration.
The following sections should be understood accordingly.
With single-minded devotion,
I take refuge in and entreat the Mahāyāna *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the ocean of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
With single-minded devotion,
we pay homage to Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa and Bodhisattva Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
The Bodhisattva Kancanagarbha,
the eternally compassionate Dharmottara, and all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time throughout the entire *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
The assembly of noble Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas,
and Sages, with one mind, reverently entreats:
Homage to the Great Brahmā, Honored Deva.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three,
the Four World-Protecting Kings,
and Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada.
